title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
official_title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
summary: This law amends the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016. Its central provision, a new subsection 5(f), says that for any claim that is otherwise timely under that Act, all defenses or substantive doctrines based on the passage of time — laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription and usucapion — may not be applied, and neither may any non-merits discretionary basis for dismissal, including the act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, prudential exhaustion and similar doctrines unrelated to the merits. Congress states its reason in a finding this law inserts into the 2016 Act: some courts, it says, have frustrated that Act's intent by dismissing recovery lawsuits in reliance on those defenses, and it names Zuckerman, Cassirer and Von Saher as its examples. A new subsection 5(b) deems a covered claim to be an action in which rights in violation of international law are in issue for purposes of section 1605(a)(3) of title 28, without regard to the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim. The 2016 Act's own sunset is struck, its closed filing window ending December 31, 2026 is replaced by claims filed on or after that Act's enactment, and every change applies to claims already pending in any court, including on appeal.
brief: Bars time-based and non-merits defenses against otherwise-timely Nazi-looted art claims, lets them proceed without regard to the victim's nationality notwithstanding the domestic-takings rule of Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, strikes the 2016 Act's sunset, and reaches cases already pending.

top_lines.headline: Procedural Defenses Eliminated
subs: For any claim that is otherwise timely under the 2016 Act, laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription and usucapion may not be applied — nor may the act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, prudential exhaustion or similar doctrines unrelated to the merits
Applies to any claim pending in any court on the date of enactment, including one pending on appeal or for which the time to file an appeal has not expired

top_lines.headline: Relation to Foreign State Immunities
subs: A covered claim is deemed an action in which rights in violation of international law are in issue for purposes of section 1605(a)(3) of title 28, without regard to the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim — the finding names the domestic-takings rule under Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp as what this displaces

Nationwide service of process added: process may be served in the district where the case is brought or any other district of the United States where the defendant may be found, resides, has an agent, or transacts business

top_lines.headline: Sunset and Filing Window Removed
subs: The 2016 Act's sunset, under which the whole Act would have ceased to have effect on January 1, 2027, is struck outright
The closed filing window ending December 31, 2026 is replaced by claims filed on or after the 2016 Act's enactment; that Act's six-year actual-discovery rule is left in place

items.main: Names the Act the “Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Adds a new subsection 5(f) to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016. It operates only on a claim that is otherwise timely under that Act, and on such a claim it bars all defenses or substantive doctrines based on the passage of time and all non-merits discretionary bases for dismissal.
items.detail: Prohibited time-based defenses include laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, and usucapion. Prohibited non-merits defenses include the act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, and prudential exhaustion. The bill adds findings naming specific court decisions that frustrated the original Act's intent, including Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art (2d Cir. 2019), Cassirer v. Thyssen-Bornemisza Foundation (9th Cir. 2024), and Von Saher v. Norton Simon Museum of Art (9th Cir. 2018).

items.main: New Section 5(b) deems Holocaust art claims to constitute actions involving violations of international law for purposes of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3)), regardless of the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim.
items.detail: This directly overrides Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, 592 U.S. 169 (2021), in which the Supreme Court held that the "domestic takings" rule barred FSIA jurisdiction over property seized from a country's own nationals. Nationwide service of process is added for all civil actions under the Act. All amendments apply to claims pending on the date of enactment — including cases pending on appeal or within the appeal filing window — and to cases filed after enactment.

items.main: Strikes the 2016 Act's sunset subsection outright and replaces its closed filing window, which ended December 31, 2026, with claims filed on or after that Act's enactment.
items.detail: The 2016 Act carried two separate time limits. Its sunset provided that the Act "shall cease to have effect on January 1, 2027", subject to an exception for claims already pending on that date; S. 1884 strikes that subsection. Separately, its applicability provision reached claims filed "during the period" ending December 31, 2026; that phrase is struck and replaced with "on or after the date of enactment of this Act" — and because the replacement is inserted into the 2016 Act, the enactment it points at is the 2016 one. The six-year actual-discovery rule in that Act is not touched.

underreported.summary: The law applies to any civil claim pending in any court on the date of enactment, including claims pending on appeal and claims for which the time to file an appeal has not yet expired.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is the permanent removal of procedural barriers to future claims. The retroactive reach to cases already dismissed and currently on appeal means courts that previously dismissed Holocaust art claims on laches or international comity grounds could have those dismissals challenged or reversed under the new law, affecting outcomes in litigation already underway.

underreported.section: The 2016 Act's Own Confidence in Private Settlement, Downgraded
underreported.summary: The law also rewrites one of the 2016 Act's findings about alternative dispute resolution, striking "will yield just and fair resolutions in a more efficient and predictable manner" and inserting "may, in some circumstances, yield just and fair resolutions as well".
underreported.why_unreported: It is a one-clause edit inside a findings section, so it carries no operative force on its own — but it is Congress stepping back from its own 2016 assessment that negotiated settlement outside court was the better route, in the same law that removes the defenses which had been pushing claimants toward that route.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Raskin
featured_quotes.text: This bill, which has already passed the Senate by unanimous consent, amends the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016 in a number of key ways to ensure that Holocaust survivors and their heirs have a fair opportunity in court to recover all of the artwork that was stolen by the Nazi regime or what is left of it. In doing so, this bill will provide these victims the chance to obtain some small measure of justice for the horrors and the injustices and indignities their families have endured.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: it is just for Holocaust survivors and their heirs to continue to have their claims relating to art stolen from them  by the Nazis heard in court. These claims should be decided on the merits, not dismissed due to technical defenses. The Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025 will ensure just that.

gaps: The law bars procedural defenses but does not address the evidentiary standard for establishing provenance or Nazi-era confiscation in the underlying merits of a claim.

added: Section 5(b) of the HEAR Act — foreign sovereign immunity exception: Holocaust art claims deemed violations of international law under 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3) regardless of victim nationality

Section 5(f) — prohibition on all time-based defenses (laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, usucapion) and non-merits discretionary defenses (act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, prudential exhaustion)
Section 5(g) — nationwide service of process for Holocaust art civil actions
modified: HEAR Act of 2016 findings — expanded to name specific court decisions that frustrated the Act's intent and to state that non-merits defenses must be precluded
HEAR Act Section 3(2) — definition of covered defenses expanded to include "other non-merits defenses" alongside statutes of limitation
removed: December 31, 2026 filing deadline for Holocaust art recovery claims
Section 5(g) of the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016 — the sunset providing that the Act would cease to have effect on January 1, 2027
